summary: Specifies how to use PKCS #5 version 2.1 (RFC 8018) to derive a symmetric key from a password with the Russian national GOST algorithms. PKCS #5 repeatedly applies a pseudorandom function, such as a hash or HMAC, to the password and a salt. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A password is turned into a strong secret key by mixing it many times with salt. This tells how to do that mixing using Russia's national recipes.

questions: how to derive keys from passwords with gost
subtitle: How to derive encryption keys from passwords using Russia's national cryptographic algorithms.

tldr.problem: Passwords are weak—users cannot remember long random strings. To use a password for encryption, it must be transformed into a strong cryptographic key. RFC 8018 (PKCS #5) defines a standard way to do this called PBKDF2: apply a hash function repeatedly to the password and salt many times until a strong key emerges.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to apply PBKDF2 with the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function (a Russian national standard) to derive encryption keys. It defines which GOST algorithms to use for encryption and message authentication, and provides the necessary identifiers and parameters for interoperable implementations.
tldr.outcome: Systems that need to encrypt data using passwords can now do so with GOST algorithms in a standard, interoperable way. This is particularly relevant for organizations in Russia and other countries that mandate or prefer GOST standards.

today: RFC 9337 is an Informational RFC published in December 2022 by the IETF independently of other RFC streams. It specifies the use of PKCS #5 with GOST algorithms to facilitate interoperable implementations, particularly for organizations that mandate GOST standards in Russia and related regions.

sections.title: Passwords and Key Derivation
sections.content:
Users can remember passwords, but they cannot remember cryptographic keys—long sequences of random bytes. The solution is a key derivation function: an algorithm that takes a password (and a random salt) and produces a strong key by applying a pseudorandom function repeatedly.

RFC 8018, also known as PKCS #5, defines the PBKDF2 algorithm for this purpose. PBKDF2 repeatedly applies a keyed hash function (an HMAC) to the password and salt, with an iteration count chosen to make the computation expensive enough that brute-force attacks become impractical.

GOST algorithms are the national cryptographic standards of Russia. They define specific hash functions (GOST R 34.11-2012), encryption algorithms (GOST R 34.12-2015 with variants like Kuznyechik and Magma), and related cryptographic primitives. This RFC shows how to apply PBKDF2 with GOST hash and encryption functions, enabling interoperable implementations that comply with Russian standards.
sections.eli5: A password is weak by itself. You hash it many times with salt to make it strong. Russia has its own recipes for hashing and encryption, so this explains how to follow those recipes.

sections.title: Key Derivation with PBKDF2
sections.content:
PBKDF2 takes four inputs: a password (P), a random salt (S), an iteration count (c), and the desired output length (dkLen). It produces a derived key (DK) by computing a series of intermediate values. For each block i, it applies the HMAC in a chain: the first application mixes the password and salt with an integer counter, then each subsequent application is fed the previous result. Finally, all the intermediate values are XORed together.

The iteration count is critical: higher counts make the derivation slower and more expensive to brute-force, but also slow down legitimate users. The RFC specifies that the minimum iteration count is 1000, with recommendations to use higher values depending on the sensitivity of the data and the available compute time.

When GOST is used, the pseudorandom function is HMAC_GOSTR3411—an HMAC constructed with the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function. The salt is a random byte string of 8 to 32 octets, and the output length is typically 32 octets for encryption keys.
sections.eli5: You start with your password and salt. You hash them together, then hash the result, then hash that result, repeating hundreds or thousands of times. Each repetition makes it harder for attackers to guess the password.

sections.title: Encryption and Message Authentication
sections.content:
Once a key is derived, it can be used for encryption. This RFC specifies the PBES2 scheme (Password-Based Encryption Scheme 2): use PBKDF2 to derive a key, then use that key with the GOST R 34.12-2015 encryption algorithm in CTR_ACPKM mode (counter mode with automatic key management).

The encryption process selects a random salt and iteration count, derives a key using PBKDF2, optionally generates a random value called ukm, and encrypts the message. For certain variants, the RFC also uses a key derivation tree to create separate encryption and authentication keys from the derived key, and appends a message authentication code (MAC) before encryption.

The PBMAC1 scheme (Password-Based Message Authentication Code Scheme 1) uses the same PBKDF2 derivation to create a key for message authentication. It applies the HMAC to a message and serializes the salt and iteration count so that a recipient can verify the MAC by deriving the same key from their copy of the password.
sections.eli5: The strong key you grew from your password can now lock a message. You also save the recipe (salt and iteration count) with the locked message so the recipient can grow the same key and unlock it.

sections.title: GOST Algorithm Variants
sections.content:
The RFC specifies two GOST R 34.12-2015 encryption algorithms: Kuznyechik (also called AES-like because it uses a 128-bit block) and Magma (a 64-bit block algorithm). Each can be used in two modes: CTR_ACPKM (counter mode with periodic key rotation) for encryption alone, or CTR_ACPKM_OMAC (counter mode with one-time MAC) for combined encryption and authentication.

The choice between Kuznyechik and Magma affects the block size, performance, and security characteristics. Kuznyechik is generally preferred for new applications because of its larger block size. The RFC also specifies identifiers for each algorithm combination and the parameters required to instantiate them.

The HMAC_GOSTR3411 function used in PBKDF2 is based on GOST R 34.11-2012 with a 512-bit output, as specified in RFC 6986 and RFC 2104.
sections.eli5: Russia has a few encryption recipes (Kuznyechik is the new one, Magma is older). You can use either one, and you can add a message code check at the same time, or do it separately.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
The security of password-based encryption rests on the difficulty of guessing the password. PBKDF2's iteration count directly impacts this: more iterations slow down an attacker's brute-force attempt. The minimum iteration count of 1000 is based on 2000-era computing power; modern recommendations suggest much higher values, such as 100,000 or more, to account for faster computers.

The salt must be random and unique for each password derivation. Reusing the same salt across multiple password derivations allows an attacker to precompute a single rainbow table that works for all of them. A random salt of at least 8 octets is recommended.

GOST algorithms are evaluated in Russia and some other countries as meeting their national security requirements. However, they are not evaluated under the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) process, and their cryptographic strength is debated in the international community. Organizations should conduct a security review appropriate to their threat model before deploying GOST-based systems.
sections.eli5: A strong password plus a high repetition count plus random salt equals a key that is hard to guess. But do not reuse the salt, or attackers can build cheat sheets. And if Russia's recipes are newer than you are, ask an expert before trusting them.

sections.title: Standard Identifiers and Registered Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers several identifiers with IANA for use in cryptographic standards, configuration files, and protocol messages. These identifiers specify which PBKDF2 hash function to use, which GOST encryption algorithm to use, and the parameters required to instantiate them (salt, iteration count, and ukm value).

By registering these identifiers, the RFC enables interoperability: a system can encode the choice of algorithm and parameters in a standard way, and a recipient can parse that encoding and instantiate the correct algorithm without ambiguity or proprietary extensions.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives names to all the different recipes and ingredients so that one computer can tell another 'I used this recipe with these settings' and the other knows exactly what to do.
